articles.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
articles.summary: Researchers have detected signals from the smallest distances ever probed.
articles.content:
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in detecting particle interactions at the smallest scale ever explored, which could lead to better understanding of dark matter. This has broad implications for fundamental physics and cosmology, offering hope for new discoveries that impact our understanding of the universe.
articles.personality_title: Scientists observe particle signals at the smallest scale ever measured
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long known that dark matter exists because it affects the movement of stars and galaxies, but they have never been able to see it directly. Dark matter does not give off light or energy, making it invisible to current instruments.

**What happened** – A team of researchers smashed tiny particles together at very high energy and analyzed the pieces that flew out. Among these pieces was a particle called a beauty quark, which is smaller than an atom and lasts only a tiny fraction of a second before breaking down. The scientists detected how this quark interacted with other particles at an incredibly small scale—a billion-trillionth of a meter.

**Impact** – Detecting interactions at this tiny scale is important because some theories suggest that dark matter might influence how these particles behave. By studying these interactions, scientists get a new way to search for dark matter and understand the basic building blocks of the universe in more detail.

**What's next step** – The researchers want to collect more data to explore this tiny world further. Their goal is to discover new particles and learn how they might connect to dark matter or other unknown parts of the universe.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have measured particle signals at the smallest scale ever, opening a new path to study dark matter and the universe’s smallest building blocks.

Les scientifiques ont détecté comment ce quark interagissait avec d’autres particules à une échelle incroyablement petite – un milliardième de milliardième de mètre.

**Impact** – Détecter des interactions à cette échelle minuscule est important car certaines théories suggèrent que la matière noire pourrait influencer le comportement de ces particules. Étudier ces interactions offre une nouvelle façon de chercher la matière noire et de mieux comprendre les éléments fondamentaux de l’univers.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs veulent collecter plus de données pour explorer davantage ce monde minuscule. Leur objectif est de découvrir de nouvelles particules et de comprendre comment elles pourraient être liées à la matière noire ou à d’autres parties inconnues de l’univers.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont mesuré des signaux de particules à l’échelle la plus petite jamais atteinte, ouvrant une nouvelle voie pour étudier la matière noire et les plus petits composants de l’univers.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos observan señales de partículas a la escala más pequeña jamás medida
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos saben desde hace tiempo que la materia oscura existe porque influye en el movimiento de estrellas y galaxias, pero nunca la han visto directamente. La materia oscura no emite luz ni energía, por lo que es invisible para los instrumentos actuales.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de investigadores chocó partículas muy pequeñas a muy alta energía y analizó los fragmentos que salieron. Entre ellos estaba un quark belleza, una partícula más pequeña que un átomo que dura solo una fracción de segundo antes de descomponerse. Los científicos detectaron cómo este quark interactuaba con otras partículas a una escala increíblemente pequeña: una milmillonésima de billonésima de metro.

**Impacto** – Detectar interacciones a esta escala tan pequeña es importante porque algunas teorías sugieren que la materia oscura podría influir en el comportamiento de estas partículas. Estudiar estas interacciones ofrece una nueva forma de buscar la materia oscura y entender mejor los componentes básicos del universo.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores quieren reunir más datos para explorar más este mundo tan pequeño. Su objetivo es descubrir nuevas partículas y entender cómo podrían estar relacionadas con la materia oscura u otras partes desconocidas del universo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los científicos han medido señales de partículas a la escala más pequeña jamás explorada, abriendo un nuevo camino para estudiar la materia oscura y los componentes más pequeños del universo.
